w: What's tested The molecular associations he said you need ("you do need to know the molecular associations on the ones that are sort of underlined"): t(14;18) and BCL2 in follicular lymphoma, t(11;14) and cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphoma ("if you got a test question, let's say this is expressing cyclin D1, you would know this is mantle cell lymphoma"), t(8;14) and MYC in Burkitt lymphoma, t(9;22) and the Philadelphia chromosome in CML, and t(15;17) and PML-RARA in acute promyelocytic leukemia The categories ("I want you to know generally kind of what category things are"): which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are indolent and which aggressive, acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid; and how Hodgkin lymphoma differs from non-Hodgkin lymphoma Acute leukemia: blasts are the hallmark, and more than 20 percent blasts makes the diagnosis ("that's our threshold"), any count with a defining genetic abnormality; Auer rods mean a myeloid blast; AML in adults, ALL in young children; and the two acute leukemias "you need to know": acute promyelocytic leukemia (DIC, and an excellent cure with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide) and acute monocytic leukemia in the mouth Chronic myeloid leukemia, "the main chronic leukemia that you need to know": the Philadelphia chromosome, every stage of maturation in the blood, imatinib; and CLL/SLL, one disease of small mature B cells with smudge cells What a dentist sees: swollen gums from leukemia ("you guys may actually be the clue that a patient has leukemia"), bleeding gums, Burkitt lymphoma in the jaw, the palate destroyed by NK/T-cell lymphoma, and marginal zone lymphoma in the salivary glands ("the one you guys are going to experience the most"); and the B symptoms, "really high-yield clues" of lymphoma What he said you don't need: the CD markers and the flow cytometry details ("don't waste your time learning that kind of stuff"), the AML subtypes, the differences between the classic Hodgkin subtypes, and the ALL details beyond who gets it 1 Classifying the leukemias on two axes: acute (blasts that don't mature) or chronic (cells that still mature), and myeloid or lymphoid: AML, ALL, CML and CLL Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank He came back to maturation when he turned to leukemia, calling it "one of the important concepts". The cells go through steps of maturation in the marrow as they acquire their function, and the neutrophil line, which his objectives ask for, shows it best: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, and finally the segmented neutrophil, or PMN. The myeloblast is the youngest cell: very fine chromatin, prominent nucleoli and darker blue cytoplasm. In the promyelocyte the chromatin is still fine, the cytoplasm is less dark, and granules appear. In the myelocyte the chromatin turns clumped and coarse, the nucleus starts to indent, and the cytoplasm is less blue. In the band the nucleus is indented even more and the cytoplasm turns pink, and in the segmented neutrophil the nucleus is pinched into lobes. Only the neutrophils are released into the blood. (Aloud he went from the myelocyte straight to the band; his slide puts the metamyelocyte, with its kidney-shaped nucleus, between them.) 2 Acute versus chronic leukemia (onset, course, blasts, platelets, organomegaly) and leukemia's clinical consequences: marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, infection) and cells growing in tissues (bone pain, spleen, liver, nodes, and the gums, where a dentist may be the first clue) Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Marrow failure, as the leukemic cells crowd out normal blood-making: anemia, with fatigue, malaise and pallor; bruising and bleeding from too few platelets; and fever and infections from too few working white cells. Who Usually children and the young Usually middle-aged and older Onset Rapid Insidious Course if untreated Less than 6 months 2 to 6 years Cells Immature cells: blasts Mature cells Blasts More than 20 (up to 95) percent of the marrow; more than 5 (up to 95) percent of the blood Fewer than 20 percent, in marrow and blood White count Usually increased, from the blasts, but variable Increased Anemia Mild to severe Mild Platelets Low to very low Normal to increased early, then decreased Organs Mild organomegaly Prominent organomegaly Treatment Chemotherapy, bone marrow transplant Chemotherapy, possibly a transplant Death Infection or bleeding Infection or bleeding Diagnosis Blood smear, marrow exam, stains, flow cytometry, cytogenetics Blood smear, marrow, cytogenetics (the Philadelphia chromosome) 3 Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin: Hodgkin is usually localized, spreads contiguously, rarely leaves the nodes and never involves the blood, with a few large Reed-Sternberg cells; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is usually widespread, can skip node groups, often starts outside the nodes, can reach the blood, and is mostly B-cell Study guide + recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this Classic Hodgkin lymphoma is a few very large Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells, with very prominent nucleoli, scattered among reactive cells. When found Usually localized Usually widespread Where it starts Central nodes you can't see: in the chest, by the heart, in the lungs, or possibly the abdomen Peripheral nodes, or outside the nodes Spread Contiguous: from one node to the node next to it Can be non-contiguous: a node above the diaphragm and one below, with the node between them not enlarged Outside the nodes Uncommon Much more common Peripheral blood Never involved Can be involved The tumor cells A few scattered, very abnormal, bizarre cells, so it can be tricky to diagnose Look very much like normal lymphocytes, so the tests are put together Treatment ABVD Often CHOP He said the main Hodgkin lymphoma is classic Hodgkin lymphoma: "You don't need to know the non-classical." It is different from the rest. The tumor cells are a small fraction of the mass, sparse and very large, embedded in a reactive background rich in immune cells. They are the Hodgkin cells (one nucleus) and the Reed-Sternberg cells (two or more nuclei), together called HRS cells. The classic Reed-Sternberg cell has two nuclear lobes, each with a prominent, eosinophilic (pink) nucleolus, which gives it an owl's-eye look. "That's the main thing that you need to recognize, is those Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells." Stains such as CD30 and CD15 light them up, but the markers aren't needed. 4 AML's diagnostic threshold (more than 20 percent blasts; any count with a defining genetic abnormality), Auer rods (a myeloid blast, never ALL), AML in adults versus ALL in children, and the conditions acute leukemia can grow out of (myelodysplastic syndrome, CML) Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this Blasts are the hallmark of acute leukemia, and more than 20 percent, in the blood or the marrow, makes the diagnosis; an AML with a defining genetic abnormality needs no set count. The number his objectives ask for is the blast threshold. He gave two ways to diagnose AML. With a specific cytogenetic abnormality, "you can diagnose AML right away. You don't even have to have 20% blasts." Without one, the blasts must be more than 20 percent, in the blood or the marrow: "That's our threshold for making the diagnosis." If the blood shows more than 20 percent, acute leukemia can be diagnosed from it; if it shows only a few, the marrow is examined. Fewer blasts than that, in a patient with abnormal counts, point to something else, such as a myelodysplastic syndrome (later in these notes). Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): persistent cytopenias with abnormal function and look of the red cell, granulocyte and/or megakaryocyte precursors. It may start with few blasts and progress to more. 5 ALL, the acute leukemia of young children (usually 1 to 5 years old, a poor prognosis under 1): B-ALL most often, and T-ALL, confirmed as T-cell by testing rather than by its look Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Aloud he added a few points to the table below: AML is relatively rare in children; ALL is usually seen at 1 to 5 years of age, with a particularly poor prognosis under 1 year; AML's blasts have a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and may or may not hold Auer rods: "If you see Auer rods, that tells you that you're looking at a myeloid blast. Lymphoid blasts do not have Auer rods." The gonads, as a site outside the marrow, are more specific to ALL, and flow cytometry tells the two apart, by markers you don't need. 6 Chronic myeloid leukemia, the chronic leukemia he said to know: BCR-ABL1 and the Philadelphia chromosome, a very high count with every stage of maturation and few blasts, chronic versus blast phase, imatinib Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this CML: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL1; a very high white count with every stage of maturation and few blasts; tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib. Its blood and marrow. The white count is high, from 12,000 to 1,000,000 per microliter, with a median of about 80,000 (the slide writes it as 12 to 1,000 times 10 to the 9th per liter). The cells are mostly neutrophils at every stage of maturation, with peaks at the myelocytes and the segmented neutrophils, not blasts. He put it as the full pattern of maturation, from early blasts all the way to neutrophils, all increased in the blood and the marrow, with a count high enough to separate it from a reactive one, such as an infection. The marrow is hypercellular, more than 95 percent cellular, with granulocytes at every stage, and his slide shows small, hypolobated megakaryocytes. The karyotype shows the Philadelphia chromosome. Its treatment. Knowing the abnormal signal led to drugs that block it, the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, of which imatinib (Gleevec) was the first and is first-line therapy. It targets the enzymatically active part of the p210 BCR-ABL1 protein: it competes with ATP for the active site and so prevents the kinase from activating. He put it as blocking the binding site, so BCR-ABL1 can't bind its substrate and drive the cell to proliferate. In this era of kinase inhibitors, the most important sign of prognosis is the response to treatment, measured in the blood count, the chromosomes and the molecular test. 7 CLL/SLL: one disease of small, mature B cells, named by where it is (blood or node); soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells; at least 5 times 10 to the 9th B cells per liter for CLL, below that monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis; older patients, infections, largely incurable Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank CLL is diagnosed from the blood: a B-cell count of at least 5 times 10 to the 9th per liter (5,000 per microliter), with the typical look and markers. The look, which his objective stresses "particularly in blood": small lymphocytes with clumped chromatin, a pattern compared to cracked mud or a soccer ball, and many smudge cells, fragile lymphocytes that have burst apart as the smear is made. "That's a clue right away, I'm looking at that, I'm thinking CLL." The marrow can be involved in various patterns, which he said you don't need to know. In a lymph node the small cells infiltrate diffusely, with pale areas of larger cells called proliferation centers. 8 Burkitt lymphoma: very aggressive and very fast-growing, t(8;14) and MYC, the starry sky of macrophages eating debris, the jaw, EBV, and excellent survival with chemotherapy Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Burkitt lymphoma's starry sky is macrophages eating the debris of tumor cells that proliferate very fast; it carries t(8;14), MYC with IGH. Under the microscope: sheets of uniform, medium-sized, cohesive blue cells, with many tingible-body macrophages scattered among them. These macrophages have eaten the debris of tumor cells that died by apoptosis, and their pale cytoplasm against the dark blue sheet gives the classic starry-sky pattern, which he compared to Van Gogh's painting and called "the key morphologic finding in making this diagnosis". With modern immunochemotherapy including rituximab, in high-resource settings, the prognosis is excellent: overall survival over 90 percent in children and 80 percent in adults. He said that is why the diagnosis matters: the chemotherapy works. 9 Mantle cell lymphoma: from the follicle's mantle zone, t(11;14) (nothing else among the lymphomas carries it), the cyclin D1 stain, older adults with enlarged nodes, survival much longer than it was Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Cyclin D1, switched on by t(11;14), means mantle cell lymphoma; he said nothing else among the lymphomas carries t(11;14). Its genetic hallmark, and the first event in its development, is the translocation between chromosomes 11 and 14, t(11;14), present in at least 95 percent of cases. It switches on cyclin D1, and his slide calls the cyclin D1 stain diagnostic. He said the translocation "tells me right away, I'm looking at mantle cell lymphoma. Nothing else in the lymphomas will do that." Its cells carry CD5, like CLL/SLL's, so he needs another marker to tell them apart: cyclin D1, found by immunohistochemistry, not flow cytometry. "If you got a test question, let's say this is expressing cyclin D1, you would know this is mantle cell lymphoma." 10 Mycosis fungoides, the most common skin lymphoma, an indolent T-cell lymphoma (patches, then plaques, then tumors), and Sézary syndrome, its aggressive form (erythroderma, nodes and cerebriform Sézary cells in the blood) Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank He went through these quickly: "I'm not going to go over in much detail, but know that these are the most common types of cutaneous lymphomas that are involving the skin, and that they have an indolent course." Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin; with Sézary syndrome it is the most common type of cutaneous lymphoma, more than half of cases. Its lesions evolve in sequence: patches, then plaques, then tumors. They can be one or many; when localized they favor sun-protected skin, the flexures (armpits and groin) and the lower trunk and buttocks, a "bathing-trunk" distribution. Under the microscope, small to medium-sized T cells with a clear halo and hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted ("cerebriform") nuclei line up along the basal layer and infiltrate the epidermis: they are epidermotropic. The course is indolent, over years or decades, with lesions that persist and grow slowly. It can appear at any age, peaking in the late fifties. Sézary syndrome is defined by a triad: erythroderma (red skin over most of the body), generalized lymphadenopathy, and clonal T cells with cerebriform nuclei, Sézary cells, in the skin, the lymph nodes and the peripheral blood. He called it the aggressive version, with the blood and the nodes involved; the cerebriform nuclei in the blood help confirm it, and the node involvement can be subtle. Unlike mycosis fungoides, it is aggressive: the 5-year survival is 10 to 30 percent, and most patients die of opportunistic infections. 11 The other B-cell lymphomas and their associations: follicular lymphoma's t(14;18) and BCL2, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (about 30 percent, de novo or transformed), and marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, the one dentists will see most, with its infections and autoimmune links Study guide + recording · 8 questions in the bank Know this Marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma: indolent, in the salivary glands and ocular adnexa, linked to H. pylori, Chlamydia psittaci, Sjögren syndrome and Hashimoto thyroiditis, with lymphoepithelial lesions as its key finding. Most patients already have widespread disease when it is found: nodes both near the surface and deep in the chest and abdomen, and an enlarged spleen; the marrow is involved in 40 to 70 percent (he said fairly commonly), and occasionally the blood. Yet patients are often asymptomatic, and B symptoms are uncommon. It is indolent: the median survival is more than 17 years with current treatment. But it keeps progressing over time, with no plateau in the survival curves, and the prognosis is closely tied to how far it had spread at diagnosis. Stomach Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection Skin (primary cutaneous) Borrelia burgdorferi Ocular adnexa Chlamydia psittaci Salivary gland Sjögren syndrome, which commonly comes first Thyroid Hashimoto thyroiditis, which commonly comes first 12 The two acute leukemias he said you need: acute promyelocytic leukemia (t(15;17) PML-RARA, maturation stopped at the promyelocyte, DIC, cured by all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide) and acute monocytic leukemia, which can show in the gums Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this APL: t(15;17) fuses PML with RARA and stops maturation at the promyelocyte; know it for its DIC, which can kill, and for its excellent cure with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide. Acute monocytic leukemia can show outside the marrow in the mouth, as swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells. He named two acute leukemias "you need to know", and this is the first. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a type of AML in which abnormal promyelocytes predominate. Its genetic hallmark is a balanced translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17, t(15;17), which fuses the promyelocytic leukemia gene, PML, with the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene, RARA. The fusion protein, PML-RARA (written with a double colon on the slides), causes the disease by impairing myeloid differentiation: maturation stops at the promyelocyte. Patients present with symptoms of their cytopenias, with disease outside the marrow, or both, and the oral cavity is one of those places. AML that forms a mass outside the marrow is called a myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary AML). In the mouth it shows as gingival hypertrophy: swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells. His slides cite two case reports, one of them a myeloid sarcoma of the mandibular gingiva that was the relapse of a treated AML. This is what his objective means by the extramedullary presentation of acute leukemia. He said a biopsy of those gums can look a little like lymphoma, but studies confirm the leukemia, and the marrow is diffusely full of blasts. 13 The other T- and NK-cell lymphomas: peripheral T-cell lymphoma (very aggressive, B symptoms, a poor response to chemotherapy) and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (EBV, necrosis, a perforated palate) Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is a lymphoma of NK-cell or T-cell lineage that damages and destroys blood vessels, with prominent necrosis, and a very strong association with EBV. It begins in the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, Waldeyer ring or epiglottis. From the nose it can grow out into the face or erode the nasal floor, destroying and perforating the hard palate, the picture once called "lethal midline granuloma". A dentist may be the first to see it. He covered it briefly, as time ran short ("you guys may come across this"): EBV-associated lymphomas of the midline of the palate, perforating lesions from a very aggressive lymphoma causing necrosis. 14 Lymphoma categories, his closing point: which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are indolent and which aggressive, and the part of the follicle each B-cell lymphoma comes from Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank B-cell CLL/SLL, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma T-cell or NK-cell Mycosis fungoides Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, Sézary syndrome, extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma 15 Diagnosing lymphoma: the tissue makes the diagnosis (the B symptoms, high-yield clues, only raise the suspicion); an effaced node; flow cytometry shows the lineage and, with only kappa or only lambda, a clonal population; staging, with disseminated disease as stage 4 Recording + objectives · 5 questions in the bank He set a normal lymph node beside a pathologic one. To the eye, a normal node is well circumscribed and rubbery; a lymphoma node is fleshy and plump, not circumscribed. Under the microscope a normal node has B-cell areas in its outer part, the cortex, with primary follicles and germinal centers, T-cell areas deeper in, and open (patent) sinuses between them, where the macrophages live and the lymphocytes pass in and out: patent sinuses are a clue that the node is benign. In a lymphoma the architecture is altered, or effaced: replaced by tumor cells, often one monotonous population. The lab reads the tissue three ways: the routine H and E stain for morphology; immunohistochemistry, antibodies that stain proteins in the section; and flow cytometry, which reads living cells one at a time in suspension. The H and E, purple and red, gives the baseline: normal or abnormal. If it looks abnormal, the extra studies ask whether it is a lymphoma and which one. Immunohistochemistry is an antibody to part of the cell that turns it brown: one stain lights up B cells, another looks for something abnormal on them. His example of something abnormal: the light chains kappa and lambda. Each B cell carries only one of them, and a normal node has both, about 3 kappa to 1 lambda. A lymphoma's cells all come from one abnormal cell, so they show only kappa or only lambda: "that's a clue that I'm looking at something that's what we call clonal." 16 Plasma cell neoplasms: a solitary plasmacytoma versus multifocal myeloma in the marrow, rouleaux from the excess antibody, the M-spike, lytic bone, high calcium, kidney damage and anemia (CRAB) Recording + objectives · 3 questions in the bank He went through the findings: lytic bone lesions (punched-out holes in the bone on radiographs); an M-spike on protein electrophoresis, the monoclonal protein as one tall, narrow band; the CRAB features of organ damage, which stand for hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions; and rouleaux on the blood smear, red cells stacked like coins, because the large amount of immunoglobulin protein makes them stick together ("it makes this sticky"). Aloud he listed the clinical findings as hypercalcemia, renal impairment and anemia, with the lytic bone; the CRAB chart on his slide is a picture. In the jaw, myeloma's lytic lesions are radiolucencies and its calcium is high, so it can look like the brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism from Lecture A. The monoclonal protein, the rouleaux and the anemia point to myeloma. Also flagged in class From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Borak's lecture. Place the four leukemias on two axes (acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid) and know each one's look: AML's blasts and Auer rods, ALL in young children, CML's Philadelphia chromosome, CLL's smudge cells. Know the two ways leukemia does harm (marrow failure: anemia, bleeding, infection; infiltration: spleen, liver, nodes, bone, gums), Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin (Reed-Sternberg cells and contiguous nodes above the diaphragm, versus mostly B-cell and often extranodal), and the lymphomas by their associations: Burkitt (t(8;14), MYC, EBV, the jaw), mantle cell (t(11;14), cyclin D1), mycosis fungoides (patches, plaques, tumors) and Sézary syndrome (erythroderma, nodes, Sézary cells in the blood). The B symptoms: a fever of 38 °C or higher, drenching night sweats that soak the sheets, and unexplained loss of at least 10 percent of body weight in 6 months; they raise the suspicion, and the tissue makes the diagnosis. Swollen gums from leukemic cells growing in them can be the first sign of a leukemia nobody has found yet; with fatigue, pallor and bruising, get a blood count. His closing summary: know each disease's category (B or T, indolent or aggressive, acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid) and its molecular association: t(14;18) follicular, t(11;14) mantle cell, t(8;14) Burkitt, t(9;22) CML, t(15;17) APL; not the markers. You can skip Skip the individual CD markers; know that flow cytometry reads the surface antigens to tell B, T or myeloid, mature or blast, and something abnormal, such as a clone with only kappa or only lambda. Skip the AML subtypes (M0 to M7) and the subtype lists of AML and ALL; know AML versus ALL, and the acute leukemias he named. Skip the differences between the classic Hodgkin subtypes (and the non-classical type, which he also said you don't need); recognize the Reed-Sternberg cells. Know only the gist he gave: a very aggressive T-cell lymphoma, usually with B symptoms, that doesn't necessarily respond to chemotherapy. Mycosis fungoides: know that it is the most common lymphoma of the skin, a T-cell lymphoma with an indolent course, and that Sézary syndrome is its aggressive form, with the blood and nodes involved. For B-ALL and T-ALL, know who gets them: mostly children (usually 1 to 5 years, poor prognosis under 1), less often adults; T-ALL is confirmed as T-cell by testing.
